s09.slug: TUESDAY · 6:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — ZERO
body: Day seven.

He has been awake since four. He lies on his back on top of the blanket with his hands folded on his stomach and watches the ceiling come up out of the dark a piece at a time: the sprinkler head first, then the water stain over the door that’s shaped like Lake Erie with a bite out of it, then the crucifix on the wall above his own head, the arms first. Out there nothing moves. The eucalyptus in the courtyard hangs every leaf straight down, and the sky behind it is clear to the top, still more ink than blue, and there’s a bloom of cold along the bottom of the glass where the radiator doesn’t reach. His hands have stopped going to the pocket first thing when he wakes. That’s new since the weekend. What hasn’t stopped is the other thing, the one that woke him at four and has been sitting on the end of the bed since, patient as a relative.
The RAZR goes off on the desk, one buzz against the wood, and he’s across the room and has it open while the desk is still humming.

body: He sits on the edge of the bed with the phone open on his knee, the screen the only light on his side of the room. She’s at a gate in Vancouver with her bag between her boots and a coffee she won’t finish, two weeks of somebody else’s life coming off her a pin at a time, and by six o’clock tonight she’ll be standing on her own porch. A minute between the zero and the rest of it. He can see her looking at the zero for that minute before she decided it needed company.
Across the room Theo is lying on his side in the blazer with his eyes open. He watches Jack type, and says nothing.

response: He shuts the phone and lies back down with it closed in his fist on the blanket, and the ceiling finishes getting light without any help from him.
Theo turns over and faces the wall. In 412 it’s the only door he can close for somebody.
He looks at the zero on the little screen for a long time. It’s a circle. There’s nothing inside it at all.

s10.slug: TUESDAY · 11:00 AM · MORRO HALL 1100 — UNDER THE EXIT SIGN
body: Eleven o’clock sun comes in through the slot windows along the top of Morro 1100 and lies in bars across the upper tiers, and a hundred people Jack doesn’t know sit in the bars with their laptops open to Facebook and their coffees on the floor between their feet. A girl two seats down is knitting something long and purple. The boy in front of him is watching a dog ride a skateboard with the sound off, over and over, studying it like game tape. Jack climbs to the back row under the exit sign, where the two of them have sat since January, and takes his seat.

Hers is beside it, the fold-down desk folded up. He puts nothing on it. Not his bag, not the Carhartt. Two minutes in, a guy with a Jamba Juice comes sideways along the back row, late, and stops at the empty seat and points at it with the straw. “Anybody?”
“Yes,” Jack says, and the guy goes on down to the end.

It’s his first time in this room in two weeks and her first time missing it in two; right now she’s somewhere over Oregon, if he has the clock right, in a window seat with her forehead on the plastic and her knees up.

Every time she’s missed one since January — a meeting in LA, a fitting, a table read — he’s taken two handouts off the stack and kept hers in the back of his notebook, and the next class she’s taken it from him and folded it into whatever script was in her bag. Somewhere in Burnaby there’s a call sheet with a diagram of the continental shelf inside it.

Dr. Fenner draws the ocean floor on the board as one long chalk line, flat and then rising. He doesn’t do slides. He talks about the sea with the fondness of somebody it has knocked down more than once.

“Out in deep water a wave doesn’t know there’s a bottom,” he says. “What’s traveling is energy, not water. The water itself mostly goes round in a circle and ends up about where it started. Then the bottom comes up — half a wavelength down, give or take, it starts to feel it — and the wave slows. The ones behind it haven’t slowed yet, so they crowd it. It gets shorter. It gets taller. That’s shoaling.” The chalk climbs. “Now the crest is riding in deeper water than the trough out in front of it, so the top outruns the bottom, and it steepens, and steepens, and past a certain point there’s nothing underneath holding it up.” He draws the crest going over: a curl, a scribble of white. “If the bottom comes up slow, it spills. If the bottom comes up fast, it plunges. A wave doesn’t know it’s going to break until the bottom’s already under it.”

“Which is why surfers understand bathymetry better than anybody in this building without ever having read a page of it,” he says, “and why not one of them can spell it.” Somebody down front asks if that’s on the midterm. Fenner says everything is on the midterm, including the question.

“And it bends,” he says. “Whatever part of the line feels bottom first slows first, so the line swings round toward the shallow water. Refraction. Off a headland the reef comes up early, the swell wraps in on the point from both sides and piles its energy there, and the bay next door gets what’s left over. If anybody’s project is a point break, that’s your first page.”

Jack writes *wraps in on the point* in the margin. He knows what it looks like from the water: flat sea all the way out, and then off the reef the sets standing up out of nothing, one after another, in the same place every time, while she stood up on the cliff path with Sol’s camera and waved her arm at the ones she wanted him to take.
At five to twelve Fenner looks up at the clock and frees the room twenty minutes early for partner conferences on the term project, and laptops start closing up and down the tiers.
“Mr. Costigan.” He calls it up the rows from the lectern, cheerful, the chalk still in his hand. “Two weeks gone, and so’s your partner. Where’s your other half?”
“In the air.”
“Then go on. Bring her Thursday.” He’s already turning to a girl at the front with a question about tides.

The handouts for absentees are on the table by the door: problem set six, on wave period, stapled to the diagram of a plunging breaker, the curl drawn with a ruler and the white water done in dots. He stops at the stack.

choices.text: *Take hers, the way you always did.*
response: He takes two off the stack and puts hers in the back of his notebook, where hers always went, behind his own, with the ruled curl of the breaker showing over the top edge of the cover.

choices.text: *Take hers, and write across the top what she missed — for after.*
response: He writes it standing at the table in his small square print — *refraction; shoaling; the bottom comes up; the point gathers it; Thurs.* — and folds it into the notebook, and doesn’t know who the after is for.
He leaves it. Halfway down the outside steps, in the noon glare off the concrete, he very nearly goes back up for it, and keeps going down.

s11.slug: TUESDAY · 12:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE OUR FATHER
body: Noon comes into St. Brendan’s sideways through the south windows and lies in long panes across the tile. No flowers on the altar. The purple is on the ambo and on Father Osei, the altar bare but for its white cloth, and the church is the size it always is and about a fifth full.

The forty who come at noon in Lent are here. A retired couple who sit on the same side every day in matching windbreakers. Two nurses in scrubs on their lunch, one still wearing her badge on a reel. A big man in a Cal Poly jacket who kneels like it costs him. A handful of students with backpacks between their feet. Jack stands at the back by the holy water, where he stood Friday for the Stations and Saturday for the vigil. In the middle of the opening prayer somebody’s phone goes off in a backpack, a marimba, and a girl in a Marisol Rowing sweatshirt dives on it and kills it and stays bent over the backpack afterward, red to the ears.

Lena is at the front. The aisle end of the second pew: her coat, the lace of the mantilla over her hair. He doesn’t try to see her face. He sees the back of her head and her shoulders under the coat, and that’s thirty pews, and he keeps his eyes on the altar.

One of the nurses reads Isaiah, fast, a reader with twenty-five minutes for lunch. The rain and the snow come down and don’t go back up till they’ve watered the earth, *so shall my word be that goes forth from my mouth; it shall not return to me void*. Gus Ferreira gives the organ a few chords for the acclamation before the Gospel, no Alleluia in it anywhere, and the forty stand.
Father Osei reads Matthew in the purple. Don’t babble. Your Father knows what you need before you ask. *This is how you are to pray.*

He doesn’t go back up for the homily. He stands at the foot of the sanctuary step with his hands folded in front of him and his eyes going along the forty and stopping nowhere. “They think they will be heard for their many words,” he says. “So He gives us a few, and trusts us with them.” He goes and sits down. The retired couple, who know him, have already opened their missalettes to the creed.
The bells at the consecration, rung by a boy of about sixty. The Great Amen, thin, forty people strong.
St. Brendan’s doesn’t hold hands at the Our Father. The forty stand with their own hands folded, or at their sides, or on the pew in front, and Father Osei opens his arms, and they begin.
*Our Father, who art in heaven* — low and uneven, the retired couple a word behind, the nurses ahead — *hallowed be thy name.*

Her voice is in it. He isn’t listening for it. He hears it anyway, from all the way down at the front under the others, the New Orleans in her vowels on *kingdom*, a little quicker than the church, the way she says everything she already knows by heart.
*Thy kingdom come; thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive —*

He stops. The church goes on without him for the rest of the line, forty people forgiving those who trespass against them in a tiled room at twelve-thirty on a Tuesday, and he stands at the back with his mouth shut and his hands at his sides. At *and lead us not into temptation* he comes back in, with them, and says the rest. Father Osei goes on alone, and the church answers him.

At the sign of peace Mrs. Fitch turns round in the last pew in front of him in her hat and gives him her gloved hand, driving gloves, kid leather gone soft at the knuckles. “Peace be with you, dear.” The man in the Cal Poly jacket leans across the aisle with a hand like a first baseman’s mitt. Down at the front hands go across the pews and back. Jack turns to the altar and keeps his eyes there.

He goes up to Communion last, from the back. By the time he passes the second pew she is already back in it, kneeling, and he passes the end of it and receives, and comes up the side aisle to the holy water and kneels on the tile there with the cool of the stone coming through his jeans. He doesn’t ask for anything. He has asked for things all week. He kneels with his hands loose on his knees in the noon from the windows, and keeps still, and offers that.

After the dismissal Father Osei is at the door in the purple, shaking hands with the forty as they go out into the noon, asking the nurse about her mother’s hip, telling the retired couple their grandson’s Confirmation name is a good one. When Jack gets to him he takes his hand, the grip of a man who used to set bones.
“Eat something, Jack.”
He lets go, and has already turned to the man in the Cal Poly jacket, who wants to know about the fish fry.

s12.slug: TUESDAY · 3:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — EGGS ACQUIRED
body: The banana he bought at the Commons after Mass is on the desk where he put it, unpeeled, starting to freckle at one end in the sun from the window. Father Osei said eat something. Skye said don’t eat. The banana is his attempt to obey them both, and it isn’t working for anybody.
She has been coming up the coast all afternoon on the outside screen.

body: He knows the stretch: the 101 coming down right onto the water past the county line, the point off to the left with a crowd of wet suits sitting on it on a clear day, the swell lined up to the horizon like somebody ironed it. She’d have had the window down. She’d have had the radio up and been singing the wrong words on purpose.

He has showered. His hair is still wet at the neck. He shaved too, and then looked in the mirror over the sink and wished he hadn’t, because it makes his face look like an occasion, and there is nothing to be done about that now but wait for it to grow. He stands at the closet thinking about what you can get eggs on, and puts on what he always puts on: the jeans, a flannel, the Carhartt over it, the boots. The same as every day she ever saw him. The RAZR goes into the breast pocket beside the pack, and he does up the button over both of them and stands there with his hand on the canvas, feeling the two corners through it, the phone’s and the box’s.

body: He can see the acquiring: the little market at the top of Del Playa, her bag still in the Saab, a carton of brown and a carton of white held up side by side under the fluorescent light while she decides which kind a frittata would want, and then buying both.
Theo is on his bed with a screenplay tented on his stomach, brads up, and hasn’t turned a page since three. He watches Jack lace the boots.
“Want me to walk you down?”
“No.”
Theo nods at the ceiling, as if it asked.

The door’s propped open for the air. Kevin goes past it in the hall with a laundry basket on his hip and a box of Tide balanced on the top, headed for the stairs and the basement, and slows, and looks in at Jack’s face.
“Jack.”
Not Costigan. The basket goes on down the hall.

s13.slug: TUESDAY · 5:35 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE LIGHT
body: Ocean Road runs down the hill to Las Olas with the sun almost in the water at the end of it, a long low gold that gets into everything and makes every parked car on the street look washed. The air hasn’t moved all day. A half moon is already up over the water, high and white and cut clean down the middle, waiting for the sky to get dark enough to be worth something.

On Las Olas two boys are walking a keg up the outside stairs of a duplex, one going backwards and swearing, the other saying *you’ve got it, you’ve got it*, and on the balcony above them a girl in a Marisol hoodie holds the screen door open with her hip and a speaker on the rail plays “Replay” turned up for a much bigger party than this one. A dog in a bandanna watches the keg from the lawn with professional interest. Two houses down somebody is grilling hot dogs on a Weber on a flat roof, and the smoke comes down across the street in the still air and hangs at head height, and he walks through it. A kid in board shorts and a parka, coming the other way with a bag of ice on his shoulder, points at Jack with his chin. “Tonight. Keg. It’s Tuesday.” He doesn’t wait for an answer. He’s happy. The street is happy about it being Tuesday.

At the corner the sun touches the water and goes, all at once, faster than it ever goes at home, where it takes all of a winter afternoon to give up behind the trees on the far side of Mill Creek Park. He has walked this street maybe forty times since October. He knows the house with the Christmas lights still up in February and the house with the fence made out of broken surfboards and the house where somebody has painted SURF OR DIE on the garage and somebody else has added AND STUDY under it in a different color. He doesn’t look at any of them. He looks at the next corner.

Del Playa goes blue as he turns onto it. On the ocean side the houses sit right on the edge of the bluff, and under their back decks the Pacific is coming in long and slow, the last of the gold laid along the top of each swell before it goes down onto the sand.
By the time he gets to the surf house the song is gone behind him, and it’s quiet enough to hear somebody winding a string.

Julian’s garage is out back of it, the door rolled up. Inside, the free piano against the back wall, the one he tuned himself, with sheet music stacked on the lid; a work lamp hung on a hook from a rafter, already on, making a yellow room of the place. A coffee mug full of picks on the piano lid. A capo clipped to the music stand like a clothespin. Julian is sitting on the step at the edge of the concrete with a guitar across his knees and a new string half on, threaded through the bridge and wound twice round the peg. One of his father’s old cardigans, brown, the elbows going. The Timex. He has the loose end of the string in his teeth.
Julian looks up.
He takes the string out of his mouth, and nods, the small one, the same nod he gave over the brass bar of the Hollis door, and goes back to the string.

response: He nods back, and keeps on down Del Playa. Behind him the string comes up to pitch, a note climbing and climbing and settling where it belongs, and then nothing more.
“Jack.” A turn of the peg; the string tightening by a hair. Nothing more is said, and nothing more needs to be. Julian bends his head to the guitar.

s13a.slug: TUESDAY · 5:52 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE FOOT OF HER STEPS
body: The smell reaches the sidewalk before he does: butter, going brown in a pan, coming out through a screen door onto a street that usually smells of kelp and spilled beer.

Sol Holm’s house sits back from the road falling down at its own pace. The porch leans left toward the neighbors. The swing hangs at the far end on its chains, not moving. Over the door the porch light is on, yellow, against a sky that isn’t quite dark enough to need it. At the curb the Saab sits with two hours of the 101 on its windshield and the dent he knows.

body.text: He has stood on this walk at two in the morning. The yellow boots are by the door where they were, the script still pushed down in the left one to the brads, and the coffee can of beach glass is on the rail with the blue piece on top. All of it the same as Saturday. He can see the colors now.
body.else: It’s the first time he’s seen her porch since the darkroom. The yellow boots by the door, a script pushed down in one of them. A coffee can of beach glass on the rail, mostly green, one blue piece on top.

body: Through the screen, faint, a record is playing, a bass walking somewhere under it, and a pan being moved on a burner.
He stops at the foot of her steps with his hands in the Carhartt’s pockets and says the Our Father for her, not loud enough for the porch to hear, slowly.

*Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.* He says it at the speed you’d say it to somebody writing it down. *Thy kingdom come; thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.* For her. He tries to keep himself out of it, and finds out how hard that is, because there’s an *us* or an *our* in every line of it. *Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive —*
He stops.
Inside, the pan scrapes. He stands at the bottom of her steps with the butter in the air and the light on over the door, and he starts it again from the top, slower.

*Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.* Slower than that. *Thy kingdom come; thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.* The bass inside walks on under it. *Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our trespasses* — and here, where it stopped, he goes on — *as we forgive those who trespass against us; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.*
Amen.

body.text: On Wednesday at Holy Rosary, with the ash still on him, he asked for the words in the right order. He has the first one.
On Wednesday at Holy Rosary, with the ash still on him, he asked that tonight wouldn’t break her. He asks it again.
On Wednesday at Holy Rosary he asked for Sunday. Sunday’s done. That one was answered.

body: He takes his right hand out of his pocket. The record goes on behind the screen. He puts his foot on the bottom step, and the board gives under it a little, the way the old ones do, and the light stays on over the door.
